name: node-addon 0.0.56 (2026-11-20)
body:
## Fixes

### Alias limits for `@fromContext` fetches

`new QueryPlanner(supergraphSdl, options)` takes optional planner options, the same ones the router reads from its config:

- `maxAliasesPerRequest`, like `traffic_shaping.all.max_aliases_per_request`
- `subgraphMaxAliasesPerRequest`, like `traffic_shaping.subgraphs.<name>.max_aliases_per_request`, by subgraph name
- `experimentalAbstractTypeFolding`, like `query_planner.experimental_abstract_type_folding`

`new QueryPlanner(supergraphSdl)` plans like before.

Every `Fetch` and `BatchFetch` with context variables now has `maxContextGroups` when there's a limit: the most groups of context values one request may carry. An executor puts up to that many groups in one request, each under its own aliases, and sends as many requests as it takes, the way the router does. `1` means one request per group, also when the fetch can't be aliased per group, so an executor no longer has to check that itself. Without it there is no limit and every group goes in one request.

name: node-addon 0.0.55 (2026-11-20)
body:
## Fixes

### Entity keys, possible types and the response projection

The `QueryPlanner` now has `entityKeys`, each subgraph's resolvable `@key`s by entity type, and `possibleTypes`, the types of each interface and union, the way the router's executor sees them. An executor no longer has to read them from the supergraph itself.

Every plan now also has its `projection`, the operation's selections merged and resolved the way the router shapes the response with them: each field with its alias, nullability, the parent types it applies to and the conditions it's projected under.

name: hive-router 0.3.19 (2026-11-20)
body:
## Features

### Automatic Persisted Queries to subgraphs

The router can send subgraph requests as Automatic Persisted Queries (APQ): only the SHA-256 hash of the query goes over the wire, in `extensions.persistedQuery`. When a subgraph doesn't know the hash yet (`PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_FOUND`), the router sends the request again with the query, so the subgraph can store it. When a subgraph answers with `PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_SUPPORTED`, or fails the hash-only request but answers the same query sent in full (a server without APQ, like GraphQL Yoga without the APQ plugin), the router sends the query instead and stops using APQ for that subgraph for 5 minutes, then tries again, so a subgraph that gets APQ later (or an old replica hit during a rollout) doesn't turn it off for good. A hash-only request that fails for another reason (auth, overload) is sent once more as a plain query, and when that fails too, APQ stays on. Mutations skip that extra try, since an error doesn't prove a mutation didn't run, and only retry on `PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_FOUND` and `PERSISTED_QUERY_NOT_SUPPORTED`. So a subgraph without APQ that only gets mutations needs APQ turned off in the config.

It's off by default. Turn it on for all subgraphs, and override it per subgraph:

```yaml
traffic_shaping:
  all:
    automatic_persisted_queries: true
  subgraphs:
    reviews:
      automatic_persisted_queries: false
```

Only queries and mutations sent over HTTP use APQ, subscriptions don't. A plugin that changes the query should do it in `on_subgraph_execute`, so the hash covers the changed query. A plugin that rewrites the request body in `on_subgraph_http_request` needs APQ off for that subgraph.

name: hive-router 0.3.18 (2026-11-20)
body:
## Fixes

### Faster query planning for large queries

Planning large queries does less work, with the same plans as before.

- Normalizing an operation copies less. On our largest test query, it makes 6.6M allocations instead of 9.1M and peaks at 212 MiB instead of 305 MiB.
- Optimizing the fetch graph skips checks that can't lead to a merge. On the same query, the fetch graph builds in 1.30 s instead of 1.96 s.

### `@requires` with a key field from another subgraph

A `@requires` field whose subgraph is keyed by a field the entity's original subgraph doesn't have can now be planned. The key is read from a fetch that has it.

### Send the router's own `Accept` header on subgraph requests

The router now sends `Accept: application/graphql-response+json, application/json;q=0.9` on regular subgraph requests, after header propagation. Before, it sent no `Accept` of its own, so a propagated client `Accept` reached the subgraph unchanged. A client sending `Accept: text/event-stream` made subgraphs that negotiate on `Accept` answer with an event stream, which the router then rejected with `SUBREQUEST_MALFORMED_RESPONSE`. Subscription requests keep their existing `Accept`.

name: node-addon 0.0.54 (2026-11-19)
body:
## Fixes

### Fetch ids and dependencies in query plans

Every `Fetch` and `BatchFetch` node in the plan now has its `id` and `dependsOn`, the ids of the fetches whose data it reads. A `BatchFetch` also has `completes`, the ids of every fetch merged into it. A fetch can start as soon as the fetches it depends on are done, the way the router schedules them, instead of waiting for its whole `Parallel`/`Sequence` wave.

The plan types also lose `operationName` on `FetchNode` and `BatchFetchNode`, which the plan never had, and gain `customScalarPaths` and the `omitFromResponse` flag of required fields, which it did have. `DeferPrimary.subselection` and `DeferPrimary.node` are `null` when missing, as the plan has them, instead of optional. The `{ kind: "ValueSetter" }` rewrite and the `FragmentSpread` required selection are gone, the plan never has them.

### `omitFromResponse` in query plans

A required field that is left out of the response is now marked `omitFromResponse` in the query plan's JSON, in camelCase like every other field, instead of `omit_from_response`.

name: hive-router 0.3.17 (2026-11-19)
body:
## Fixes

### `omitFromResponse` in query plans

A required field that is left out of the response is now marked `omitFromResponse` in the query plan's JSON, in camelCase like every other field, instead of `omit_from_response`.

### Spread new connections over all HTTP workers

The HTTP server now hands new client connections to its workers in turn. Before, it sent each connection to the less busy of two random workers. When many connections opened at once, a worker that had just been busy looked busy for all of them and could get none, so it sat idle while the other workers queued requests. With 4 workers and 50 connections opened together, one worker regularly got no connections at all.

name: hive-router 0.3.15 (2026-11-17)
body:
## Features

### Add `validation` configuration options to control input validation.

Input object variables containing unknown fields are rejected by default.

The new `validation.disable_unknown_input_fields_validation` option allows unknown fields in variables and forwards them to subgraphs unchanged. All other validation rules remain enforced, including required fields, type checks, and `@oneOf` constraints. Unknown fields are excluded from `@oneOf` field counting, and inline input values are still validated.

```yaml
validation:
  disable_unknown_input_fields_validation: true
```

The existing `ROUTER_DISABLE_INT_VALUE_RANGE_VALIDATION` environment variable also gains a configuration equivalent. The environment variable remains supported and takes precedence over the config file.

```yaml
validation:
  disable_int_value_range_validation: true
```

## Fixes

### Copy entities already in the response

An entity fetch often asks for entities an earlier fetch already put in the response. With entity reuse on, the fetch copies those into place and leaves them out of the request. When it has every entity, the subgraph isn't called at all. Off by default:

```yaml
traffic_shaping:
  entity_reuse: true
```

Or with the `ROUTER_TRAFFIC_SHAPING_ENTITY_REUSE=true` environment variable.

A fetch copies only from the fetches it waits for. It may also wait for an earlier fetch to the same subgraph that asked for the same fields, when that gives it something to copy. It never copies once the request has an error, in mutations, fields a subgraph only has through `@provides`, or entities whose representation has a missing or null field. Fetches with `@fromContext` arguments, input or output rewrites don't copy.

Closes #1730

name: node-addon 0.0.53 (2026-11-16)
body:
## Fixes

### Send an entity to its subgraph when the client uses the name of one of its key fields for something else.

In `{ t { x: id  id: y } }`, the client's `id` is a different field, so the router fetches the key `id` under an internal alias. The check for a complete key looked at `id` in the response instead, found nothing there before the entity call, and left the entity out, so `y` came back `null`. With `{ t { x: id  id: x  y } }`, the answer depended on which root fetch finished first. The check now looks at the key the representation actually read.

A required field that the planner aliased is also read only from that alias now. When it was missing, the router used to send whatever sat under the field's name instead, like the client's `price(currency: USD)` as the `price(currency: EUR)` a `@requires` asked for.

name: hive-router 0.3.14 (2026-11-16)
body:
## Features

### Run each subgraph fetch as soon as the fetches it reads from are done.

A query plan lists fetches in waves, and every fetch of a wave used to wait for the whole wave before it. In `{ topProducts { upc inStock reviews { author { name } } } }`, the authors only need the reviews, but they also waited for the `inStock` call, so a slow inventory subgraph held them up. Plans now keep which fetches each fetch reads from, and the router starts every fetch the moment those are in. Root mutation fields still run one after another, entity calls included.

## Fixes

### Send an entity to its subgraph when the client uses the name of one of its key fields for something else.

In `{ t { x: id  id: y } }`, the client's `id` is a different field, so the router fetches the key `id` under an internal alias. The check for a complete key looked at `id` in the response instead, found nothing there before the entity call, and left the entity out, so `y` came back `null`. With `{ t { x: id  id: x  y } }`, the answer depended on which root fetch finished first. The check now looks at the key the representation actually read.

A required field that the planner aliased is also read only from that alias now. When it was missing, the router used to send whatever sat under the field's name instead, like the client's `price(currency: USD)` as the `price(currency: EUR)` a `@requires` asked for.

### Set client response headers from the `on_execute` end hook

`OnExecuteEndHookPayload` has `insert_response_header`, `append_response_header`, `get_response_header` and `remove_response_header` for the client response headers aggregated during execution. The headers are written after all end callbacks run, so plugin values win over the computed `cache-control`, except that mutations and responses with GraphQL errors (including errors added in end hooks) always get `no-store, no-cache, must-revalidate`, and they are part of the shared response, so requests deduplicated by inbound request deduplication receive them too even though they never run `on_execute`.

```rust
payload.on_end(|mut payload| {
    payload.insert_response_header(
        HeaderName::from_static("cache-control"),
        HeaderValue::from_static("no-store"),
    );
    payload.proceed()
})
```

Closes #1688

### Smaller cached query plans for queries with many fragments

Cached query plans for queries that reuse fragments are much smaller and faster to build. On our largest test query, a plan went from 19.8 MB to 0.78 MB and builds 24x faster. Very large queries that used to fall back to the slower response parser now use the fast one.

name: hive-router 0.3.13 (2026-11-12)
body:
## Features

### Extract hard-coded field argument values into variables, so operations that differ only in those values share one query plan.

`{ user(id: "1") { name } }` and `{ user(id: "2") { name } }` are now planned once, as `query($_v0: ID!) { user(id: $_v0) { name } }`, instead of once per id. That keeps a client looping over IDs from pushing every other plan out of the plan cache. Subgraphs receive the values as variables instead of inline.

It's on by default. To opt out:

```yaml
query_planner:
  arguments_to_variables: false
```

### Upgrade to ntex 4

The router runs on ntex 4.8.0 instead of ntex 3. Users of the prebuilt binary or the Docker image do not need to change anything: the configuration, the HTTP and websocket APIs and VRL expressions are unchanged.

Custom plugins and custom router binaries built on the `hive-router` crate need the migration steps below. Code that uses ntex APIs directly through `hive_router::ntex`, such as building responses, writing ntex services or using ntex test helpers, follows the upstream [ntex 3 to 4 migration guide](https://github.com/ntex-rs/ntex/blob/main/ntex/migration_3to4.md).

## BREAKING: Request URLs use `ntex::url::Url`

ntex 4 represents request URLs with `ntex::url::Url` instead of `http::Uri`, and `ntex::http::Uri` no longer exists. The following APIs expose the new type:

- `RouterHttpRequest::uri` and `RouterHttpRequest::match_info` (`Path<ntex::url::Url>`)
- `ClientRequestDetails::url`, `MutableClientRequestDetails::url` and `ClientRequestDetailsView::url()`
- the coprocessor `MutableRequestState::uri`
- the `url` argument of `execute_planned_request`
- `HttpServerSpanRequest::uri()`
- `OnHttpRequestHookPayload::router_http_request.uri()`

`Url::path()` and `Url::query()` return wrapper types that do not deref to `str`, so string methods need `.as_str()`. Comparing them with a string literal and formatting them with `Display` work without changes.

```diff
-use hive_router::http::Uri;
+use hive_router::ntex::url::Url;

-if payload.router_http_request.uri.path().starts_with("/admin") {
+if payload.router_http_request.uri.path().as_str().starts_with("/admin") {

-let query: Option<&str> = payload.router_http_request.uri.query();
+let query: Option<&str> = payload.router_http_request.uri.query().map(|q| q.as_str());
```

`RouterHttpRequest::path` and `RouterHttpRequest::query_string` are still plain `&str` and avoid the new type entirely.

```diff
-let path = payload.router_http_request.uri.path();
-let query = payload.router_http_request.uri.query().unwrap_or("");
+let path = payload.router_http_request.path;
+let query = payload.router_http_request.query_string;
```

`host()`, `port_u16()` and `scheme_str()` keep their signatures. `port()` returns a different `Port` type, so use `port_u16()` when only the number is needed.

```diff
-let port = details.url().port().map(|p| p.as_u16());
+let port = details.url().port_u16();
```

APIs that still take an `http::Uri`, such as `reqwest` or `hyper`, need an explicit conversion. It can fail and it drops the fragment.

```diff
-let uri: http::Uri = details.url().clone();
+let uri = http::Uri::try_from(details.url()).unwrap_or_default();
```

Tests that build a `RouterHttpRequest` by hand create the URL with the new type.

```diff
-let uri: http::Uri = "http://example.com/graphql".parse().unwrap();
-let path: Path<http::Uri> = Path::new(uri.clone());
+let uri: ntex::url::Url = "http://example.com/graphql".parse().unwrap();
+let path: Path<ntex::url::Url> = Path::new(uri.clone());
```

## BREAKING: `on_http_request` payload type

`OnHttpRequestHookPayload::router_http_request` is a `WebRequest<()>` instead of a `WebRequest<DefaultError>`. Plugins that name the type in their own functions have to update it.

```diff
-use hive_router::ntex::web::{DefaultError, WebRequest};
+use hive_router::ntex::web::WebRequest;

-fn fingerprint(req: &WebRequest<DefaultError>) -> u64 {
+fn fingerprint(req: &WebRequest<()>) -> u64 {
```

## BREAKING: ntex timers are not `Send`

ntex timers such as `ntex::time::sleep` belong to the thread that created them, so their futures are not `Send`. A `BackgroundTask::run` future must be `Send`, so background tasks of plugins wait with tokio timers instead.

```diff
-use hive_router::ntex;
+use hive_router::tokio;

 async fn run(&self, token: CancellationToken) {
     loop {
-        ntex::time::sleep(self.interval).await;
+        tokio::time::sleep(self.interval).await;
```

## `on_end` callbacks on websocket connections run when the socket closes

The websocket handler serves the whole connection inside the request, so a websocket upgrade request finishes only when the socket closes. For such a request, the `on_end` callback returned from `on_http_request` runs after the connection closes, and changes it makes to the response are never sent, because the handshake was already answered.

Plugins that measure request durations, keep in-flight counters or set response headers on the websocket path see different results. Logic that has to run at the handshake belongs in `on_http_request` itself.

## Timers never fire early

ntex 4 timers fire at or after their deadline, up to one 16ms tick late, while ntex 3 timers could fire early. Periodic work such as supergraph polling runs at the configured interval or slightly later, never sooner.

### WebSocket `permessage-deflate`

The router supports the `permessage-deflate` extension (RFC 7692) on WebSocket connections from clients and to subgraphs. When both sides agree on the extension, messages are compressed in both directions. A side that does not support it declines the extension and the connection continues uncompressed.

It is disabled by default. Compression trades CPU and memory for bandwidth, each compressed connection uses about 420KiB for its compressor and decompressor.

The router accepts the extension from clients with `websocket.permessage_deflate`:

```yaml
websocket:
  enabled: true
  permessage_deflate: true
```

The router offers the extension to WebSocket-enabled subgraphs with `traffic_shaping.all.websocket.permessage_deflate`, and it can be overridden per subgraph:

```yaml
traffic_shaping:
  all:
    websocket:
      permessage_deflate: true
  subgraphs:
    payments:
      websocket:
        permessage_deflate: false
```

Closes #1864

### WebSocket operations can use headers from the upgrade request

Headers of a WebSocket operation come from the client, either from the `connection_init` payload or from the operation extensions. Headers set by trusted infrastructure on the HTTP upgrade request, like the `X-Real-IP` header set by a reverse proxy, never reached the per-operation stages.

The new `websocket.headers.upgrade` option lists the headers taken from the upgrade request and added to every operation on the connection:

```yaml
websocket:
  enabled: true
  headers:
    upgrade:
      - x-real-ip
```

The listed headers are taken only from the upgrade request. Values with the same name sent by the client in the `connection_init` payload or in the operation extensions are discarded, so the client cannot spoof them. The headers are visible to plugins, coprocessor stages, JWT authentication and expressions, and respect the header propagation rules.

Additionally, the `coprocessor.stages.router.request` documentation now states that for WebSocket connections the hook runs once on the upgrade request, and that the context entries it sets are visible to the per-operation stages of every operation on the connection.

Closes #1679

## Fixes

- The actual cost of demand control now counts `@cost` on input object fields when the input object comes from a variable, the same as it already did for inline values. It used to count them as 0, so the actual cost came out lower than the estimated cost.

### Conditional `@requires` inputs stay with their condition

A `@requires` field under `@skip`/`@include` next to an unconditional field of the same entity, like `permissions @skip(if: $skip)` next to `basicPermissions`, no longer turns the unconditional field into `null` when the condition is off. Entity calls only merge when each side's input is there whenever the merged call runs.

### Fields missing from the response under `@include`/`@skip`

- An abstract field selected again under `@include`/`@skip` keeps its fields with the condition off. The subgraph is now asked for the `__typename` the response needs to tell the types apart, not only under the condition.
- A field under a fragment on every type its parent can be, like `... on Query @include(if: $a) { feed { id } }` next to `feed { id }`, no longer goes missing from the response.

### Interface entity calls only send the types they ask for

An entity call through an interface key, like `Animal @key(fields: "id")`, sent every implementation, even when everything it asked for was under `... on Dog` and `... on Cat`. Birds went to the subgraph with nothing to resolve.

- Such calls now only send the types the selection asks for, each with its own `__typename` (`"Dog"`, not `"Animal"`). Data from an `@interfaceObject` is sent as before.
- An entity is no longer sent as `__typename` alone, which no subgraph can resolve, unless one of its keys is `__typename` alone.

### Keep `@include`/`@skip` conditions on entity calls

The query planner could lose a condition on its way down to an entity call, so the call ran with the condition off and the subgraph resolved entities nobody asked for. This happened with a fragment condition when a child has a condition of its own, and with batched calls under a type condition, for the types the path doesn't name.

A same-type fragment's condition now also moves to its inner fragments, so those entities are looked up once instead of twice.

A conditional same-type fragment under an interface that's an `@interfaceObject` elsewhere no longer fails planning with `NoPathsFound`.

### Persisted documents file watching follows symlinks

The persisted documents file watcher reloads the manifest when its path goes through a symlinked directory, such as the temp directory on macOS. File system events on macOS report resolved paths, so the watcher matches events against both the configured and the canonicalized manifest path.

### Entity calls keep the conditions they were planned under

An entity call under nested `@include`/`@skip`, like `orders @include(if: $a) { ... on Order @include(if: $b) { name } }`, only kept the innermost condition and relied on the call above it for the rest. When another branch fetched the same objects, or the call merged with an unconditional sibling, it ran with the outer condition off. Every call now keeps all the conditions it was planned under.

### Send the key of the right subgraph to a `@requires` field

The entity call for a `@requires` field sent the key of whichever subgraph came first, not one of the subgraph that has the field. With `Item @key(fields: "group { id }")` in one subgraph and `Item @key(fields: "group { tag }")` in the one with the field, the call sent `group { id }`, so the subgraph couldn't find the item. It now sends that subgraph's own key.

### Keep `null` list items in `@requires` representations

A list a `@requires` reads, like `similar: [Book]` in `@requires(fields: "similar { id }")`, lost its `null` items on the way to the subgraph. `[null, {id: "2"}, null, {id: "3"}]` arrived as `[{id: "2"}, {id: "3"}]`, so a resolver that counts the items or reads their positions got the wrong answer. Every item now keeps its place, and one with nothing to send is sent as `null`.

### - Reduce synchronization overhead when cloning supergraph snapshots and generating request IDs.

- Skip external wait tracking when the corresponding telemetry metrics are disabled
- Enable `TCP_NODELAY` for subgraph HTTP connections
- Serialize GraphQL variables directly into request buffers, avoiding intermediate allocations
- Speed up response projection and object lookups with optimized field name comparisons

Closes https://github.com/graphql-hive/router/issues/1781

### Faster reading of subgraph responses

The router now reads each subgraph response with the shape of the query it sent. It knows which fields to expect and in what order, so it skips most of the work a general JSON parser does. Responses it isn't sure about are read the old way, so the results and errors stay the same. In our benchmark the router uses about 7% less CPU per request.

### Query planner, projection and demand control fixes

- Entities inside lists of lists (`[[Product]]`, `[[[Product]]]`) are resolved. They used to come back as `null` without an error.
- An object inside a representation that misses a selected field is sent as `null` instead of without that field.
- A conditional fragment on a union field's own union type, like `... on Component @skip(if: $v)`, no longer fails with `NoPathsFound`.
- The same `@fromContext` field selected twice in one entity call shares one context variable, instead of sending one response key with two different arguments, which the subgraph rejects.
- Demand control applies `@include`/`@skip` on inline fragments when estimating cost.
- Demand control counts the fields of a conditional fragment on an interface or union, like `... on Product @include(if: $v)`, in the actual cost. They were left out.
- Demand control counts every object of a list of lists, like `[[Product]]`, and its fields in the actual cost, instead of one per inner list.

name: graphql-tools 0.5.13 (2026-11-12)
body:
## Fixes

### Lists of different lengths are different values

`OverlappingFieldsCanBeMerged` treated a list argument and any prefix of it (`[]` included) as the same value, so `f(input: ["a"])` and `f(input: [])` could share a response key.

### Object literals are checked outside input object positions

`ValuesOfCorrectType` only checked an object literal where an input object was expected, so `{ field(arg: { a: 1 }) }` passed validation even when `arg` is a `String`. An object literal anywhere else is now checked like any other value. Custom scalars still accept them.

name: hive-router 0.3.12 (2026-11-03)
body:
## Fixes

### Batch conditional entity fetches

Entity fetches under `@include`/`@skip` used to go out as separate requests. They're now batched with the other entity fetches to the same subgraph, so operations with many conditional fields send far fewer requests.

A fetch whose condition is false sends no entities, and if every fetch in the batch is off, no request is sent. Demand control only counts the fetches that run.

name: hive-router 0.3.11 (2026-11-03)
body:
## Features

### Support `https://` coprocessor URLs

`coprocessor.url` now accepts `https://` endpoints, and a new `coprocessor.tls` block configures how the router connects to them. It takes the same settings as `traffic_shaping.subgraphs.<name>.tls`: a custom CA (`cert_file`), a client certificate for mTLS (`client_auth`), and `insecure_skip_ca_verification`.

```yaml
coprocessor:
  url: https://coprocessor.internal:8443/hook
  protocol: http2
  tls:
    cert_file: ./certs/coprocessor-ca.pem
    client_auth:
      cert_file: ./certs/router.pem
      key_file: ./certs/router.key
```

- Without a `tls` block, the coprocessor's certificate is verified against the system's root certificates. `coprocessor.tls` does not inherit `traffic_shaping.all.tls`.
- `protocol: http1` and `protocol: http2` are supported over `https://`. `http2` was previously rejected; it now requires an `https://` endpoint, and `h2c` requires `http://` or `unix://`.
- Setting `tls` on an `http://` or `unix://` endpoint fails at startup.
- The per-stage `timeout` includes the TLS handshake when a new connection is opened.

Closes https://github.com/graphql-hive/router/issues/1731

### Size HTTP server workers to the container's CPU limit

`http.workers` (and `ROUTER_HTTP_WORKERS`) now accepts `cpuset` and `container`, in addition to an explicit number of workers.

- `cpuset` (default, unchanged behavior): one worker per logical CPU the process is allowed to run on (its CPU affinity mask, which follows the cgroup cpuset on Linux). CPU limits are not taken into account, so in Kubernetes this is usually the number of CPUs of the node.
- `container`: like `cpuset`, but also capped by the container's CPU limit (the cgroup CPU quota), rounded down, with a minimum of `1`. For example, a `1500m` CPU limit results in a single worker.
- A positive integer: an explicit number of workers, as before.

```yaml
http:
  workers: container
```

Closes https://github.com/graphql-hive/router/issues/1561

## Fixes

### Faster entity merging

## Features

### Don't send a fetch whose fields are all skipped

A fetch whose fields are all switched off by `@include`/`@skip` on different variables, like `details @include(if: $d)` and `inventory @include(if: $i)` with both off, is no longer sent ([#1733](https://github.com/graphql-hive/router/issues/1733)). It used to go out with nothing to resolve, and the subgraph still loaded each entity.

`FetchNode` in the query plan gets an optional `runIf`, a list of condition groups. The fetch runs when any of them holds, and always when it's missing. Each group has `includeIf` and `skipIf` variable names, and holds when every `includeIf` variable is `true` and no `skipIf` one is. Demand control only costs a fetch when it runs.

`runIf` also has the `@include`/`@skip` around the fetch, so query plans no longer have `Condition` nodes. A fetch under `... @include(if: $a)` is now `Fetch(service: "b", if: $a)` instead of `Include(if: $a) { Fetch(service: "b") }`. Anything else that executes these plans has to check `runIf`.

A fetch that can never run, like one under `... @skip(if: $a) { ... @include(if: $a) { ... } }`, is left out of the plan, so `runIf` is never empty. When that leaves no fetch at all, the plan has no node.

A fetch with a `runIf` isn't batched with other entity calls for now.

Closes #1733

- Add validation options to control `Int` value range validation.

## Features

- Add an opt-in `ROUTER_DISABLE_INT_VALUE_RANGE_VALIDATION` environment variable to disable GraphQL `Int` range validation.

### `traffic_shaping.http_client_mode` with a per-worker option

Every worker of the router runs its own single-threaded runtime, but all of them shared one HTTP client and connection pool to subgraphs. A connection opened on one worker got picked up by requests on the others, so a subgraph response often had to wake up another thread.

With `http_client_mode: per_worker`, each worker gets its own client, so a request stays on its worker from start to end. In our benchmark, the router used 9.5% less CPU per request. Each worker keeps its own idle connections, so more connections can stay open, while `max_connections_per_host` still caps the requests in flight.

`shared` is the default and keeps one client for all workers.

```yaml
traffic_shaping:
  http_client_mode: per_worker
```

A fetch whose fields are all switched off by `@include`/`@skip` on different variables, like `details @include(if: $d)` and `inventory @include(if: $i)` with both off, is no longer sent ([#1733](https://github.com/graphql-hive/router/issues/1733)). Closes #1733

## Fixes

- Add validation options to control `Int` value range validation.

### Break response compression ties by the configured `algorithms` order

When a client accepted several algorithms with the same q-value, the router picked whichever the client listed first, so the order of `traffic_shaping.router.compression.response.algorithms` never acted as the documented tie-breaker. Cloudflare, for example, fetches the origin with `Accept-Encoding: gzip, br`, so the router always answered with gzip, even with `br` first in `algorithms`.

The listed order in `Accept-Encoding` carries no preference (RFC 9110 §12.5.3), so equally acceptable algorithms are now ranked by the `algorithms` order. Client q-values still take precedence.

```yaml
traffic_shaping:
  router:
    compression:
      response:
        algorithms:
          - kind: br
          - kind: gzip
```

With this config, `Accept-Encoding: gzip, br` now gets a Brotli response, and a gzip-only client still gets gzip.

### Error paths point at what the client asked for

A subgraph error inside a field the router fetched for itself, like a `@requires` value under `_internal_qp_alias_0`, or a raw `_entities` path, had a path the client never asked for. Error paths now stop at the closest value the client asked for, and an error with no such value has no path.

Union members only ask for their own fields of a shared entity type, instead of every member's fields for every entity.

body:
## Features

### `hive_router anonymize` command

Anonymizes a supergraph and its operations with a secret key, so you can share them without revealing the schema.

```bash
hive_router anonymize keygen > anon.key
hive_router anonymize supergraph --key-file anon.key supergraph.graphql > anonymous.graphql
hive_router anonymize operation --key-file anon.key operation.graphql > anonymous-operation.graphql
```

Every type, field, argument, enum value, subgraph name, string and number goes through keyed BLAKE3, so the output is a valid supergraph that plans the same way, and nobody can reverse it without the key. The same key always gives the same names, so operations can be anonymized later on their own, without touching the supergraph again.

## Fixes

### Faster fetch graph building and batching in the query planner

- Find a fetch step to reuse by its subgraph, input type, response path and condition, instead of checking every child of the parent step.
- Compare response paths without type conditions without copying them.
- Check whether two fetch steps can be batched before the more expensive ancestor check.

name: hive-router 0.3.7 (2026-10-28)
body:
## Fixes

### Fix an empty conditional fragment in subgraph requests

Fixed an issue where the query planner could generate empty fragments when batching requests with `@include` or `@skip` directives, causing subgraphs to reject the query.

### Borrow supergraph values instead of copying them

The query planner now borrows type names, field names and selections from the supergraph instead of owning copies of them. This means fewer allocations and lower memory use.

### Speed up building the query planner graph

- Parse each `@key`, `@requires` and `@provides` selection once and share it between edges.
- Cache subgraph nodes while building the graph.
- Compute the possible types of each abstract type once and reuse them during normalization.
- Index which subgraphs resolve each root field once, instead of looking it up for every field.
- Skip types that can't have entity moves or outgoing edges, and handle enum leaves more cheaply.

### Avoid duplicate graph edges and speed up supergraph decomposition

- A type that repeats `@join__type` for the same subgraph (once per `@key`) no longer adds duplicate edges to the query planner graph.
- Supergraph decomposition groups join types and enum values by subgraph in a single pass, instead of scanning every definition once per subgraph. This was slow for supergraphs with hundreds of subgraphs.

### Faster hashing and path cloning in the query planner

- Use `ahash` for the query planner's hash maps and sets.
- Share merge path segments, so cloning a path is cheap.
- Borrow possible-type sets from the supergraph when merging batched fetch steps, instead of cloning them on every merge.

### Speed up the query planner walker and fetch graph

- Look for indirect paths only when there's an entity or interface-object move to follow, and work out the target subgraphs only when that lookup runs.
- Share path lists between work items instead of cloning them, and follow inline fragments with a single direct path.
- Merge leaves and siblings faster, and price a merged plan by measuring only the nodes the merge adds.
- Group fetch steps by a key before batching multi-type fetches, so only steps that could be batched get compared.

### Fix planning of interface fields resolvable in several subgraphs

When a field returning an interface could be resolved by more than one subgraph, and its selection had more than one inline fragment, the query planner stopped using entity jumps for every field of that interface. If the selection also needed fields from other subgraphs, planning failed with `NoPathsFound`. Those fields can now be fetched from the subgraphs that provide them.

### Track a single union member after narrowing union paths

When several subgraphs can resolve a field that returns a union, the query planner narrows the candidate paths down to the members those subgraphs share. Each remaining path stands for one union member, but it used to keep the whole shared member set. So the planner could still follow fragments on the other shared members through it. Each path now keeps only its own member.

## Features

### Add at-least-once sampling for usage reporting

As in Hive Router, the Apollo-Router plugin can now report the first operation for each unique key, even with a low `sample_rate`. Later operations with the same key follow `sample_rate`.

```yaml
plugins:
  hive.usage:
    sample_rate: 0.1 # 10% of operations will be reported
    at_least_once:
      key: # the combination of operation's name and body makes the request unique
        - operation_name
        - operation_body
      max_distinct_keys: 12000 # how many keys to track and hold in memory
```

Possible keys are `operation_name`, `operation_type` and `operation_body`. Keys are tracked in memory, up to `max_distinct_keys` (default: `100_000`). Every key takes approximately 16 bytes of memory.

Sampling and the `exclude` list of operation names are now applied by the Hive Console SDK, the same way as in Hive Router. Excluded operations are dropped before sampling, so they never take a sampling slot. Sampling is decided per report, so with `@defer` or subscriptions each response chunk is sampled on its own, instead of the whole request.

`exclude` expressions can now read the operation type from `.request.operation.type`; it used to be always empty.

body:
## Features

### Query plan types for `@context` / `@fromContext`

`FetchNode` and `EntityBatchAlias` have optional `contextRewrites` and `contextVariables` fields, and `FetchNodePathSegment` has a `"Parent"` variant.

## Fixes

### Batch contextual entity fetches and cap aliases per subgraph request

Entity fetches with different `@fromContext` argument values now combine distinct context-value groups into one subgraph request using aliased `_entities` fields, instead of sending one request per group. Each alias receives only its group's representations and contextual arguments. Responses and error paths are mapped back to the original client response shape.

The new `max_aliases_per_request` traffic-shaping option caps how many aliased `_entities` fields one subgraph request may carry. It's not set by default, and can be set globally or per subgraph.

```yaml
traffic_shaping:
  all:
    max_aliases_per_request: 15
  subgraphs:
    reviews:
      max_aliases_per_request: 5
```

The cap applies to both places where the router adds aliases:

- **Query planning.** Compatible entity fetches to the same subgraph are batched into a `BatchFetch` with one alias per fetch shape. Without a cap batches are never split, same as before. With a cap, a batch with more aliases than the cap is split into several `BatchFetch` nodes that run in parallel. A leftover single fetch stays a regular fetch.
- **Contextual argument groups.** Without a cap, all groups of a fetch go in one request. With a cap, groups are split into additional requests rather than failing the operation. For example, a regular entity fetch with 12 distinct context-value groups and a cap of `5` sends three requests containing 5, 5, and 2 groups. A single group keeps the original query unchanged. In a batched fetch every group repeats all batch aliases, so each request carries `cap / batch aliases` groups, at least one.

Higher values reduce request overhead at the cost of larger query payloads. Lower values help accommodate subgraph alias or query-complexity limits, such as graphql-armor's max-aliases rule. The number of contextual argument groups depends on the response data, so a subgraph with such a limit should always have this option set. Aliases from the client's own query are not counted. Set this option to `1` (or `0`) to send one `_entities` field per request.

Both limits are decided while planning: the planner splits batches and records how many context groups fit in one request on each fetch, so execution only splits the groups it finds in the data. Plugins that build `SupergraphOptions` themselves set the limit through the new `QueryPlannerOptions::max_aliases_per_request` (`Option<usize>`) and `subgraph_max_aliases_per_request` fields, which are filled from `traffic_shaping` when converting from the router config. The query planner's default is also no cap, so query plans produced by the node addon don't split batches either.

### Support Federation `@context` / `@fromContext`

Contextual arguments are resolved per entity from the nearest ancestor that sets the context and sent as `__context_{n}` variables. Entities whose ancestors hold different values are grouped per distinct value set, and the groups are sent as aliased `_entities` fields within the `max_aliases_per_request` limit. Query plan JSON gets `contextRewrites` on `Fetch` nodes and `BatchFetch` aliases, and a `Parent` path segment.

Closes https://github.com/graphql-hive/router/issues/1655

## Fixes

### Reduce temporary allocations during AST traversal

Avoid allocating strings for temporary names when hashing query-plan ASTs and rebuilding nullified operations.

### Respect direct-only navigation when checking key fragments

Inline fragment checks now honor `use_only_direct_edges`. When the planner checks whether an entity key can be satisfied using only direct edges, fragment branches can no longer use indirect paths through other subgraphs to appear satisfiable.

For example, consider a fragment requirement:

```graphql
... on Tagged {
  tag {
    id
  }
}
```

Suppose reaching `Tagged` requires an indirect path:

```text
Current node in subgraph A -> entity in subgraph B -> Tagged
```

Previously, the fragment check could use that path even with `use_only_direct_edges: true`, incorrectly accepting the key as locally satisfiable. Now it rejects that candidate unless a direct path exists or the current type already matches `Tagged`. Checks that allow indirect edges retain their existing behavior.

### Reduce memory usage at startup and during request execution

Reduce memory allocations and copying, lowering both idle memory usage and per-request overhead.

- Render the Laboratory page lazily, avoiding unnecessary memory usage when Laboratory is not accessed.
- Transfer response bodies to ntex without copying their buffers.
- Read subgraph HTTP responses incrementally to allow Hyper to reuse its read buffers.
- Reduce cloning during response merging by borrowing source values and moving entities into their final destination.
- Allocate JSON objects and arrays with exact capacities during deserialization.
- Avoid allocating type names during authorization metadata traversal.

The query planner now recognizes that a fragment on a union applies to any object type that belongs to that union, in addition to matching exact types and implemented interfaces. This prevents applicable fragment branches from being discarded when resolving requirements or contextual selections.

For example:

```graphql
type User {
  id: ID!
}

type Product {
  id: ID!
}
```

Given this selection:

```graphql
... on SearchResult {
  ... on User {
    id
  }
}
```

When the current type is `User`, the outer `SearchResult` condition now matches because `User` is a union member. Previously, that condition did not match.

body:
## Features

### Read deadlines for request headers and body

A client could send the request headers and then send the body slowly, or never. The router kept its socket and buffers until `traffic_shaping.router.request_timeout`, with no limit on how many such requests it held, and enough of them got the router OOM-killed.

Two new options bound how long the router waits for an incoming request:

- `header_read_timeout`: time to receive the complete request headers. When exceeded, the connection is closed. Rounded up to whole seconds.
- `body_read_timeout`: time to receive the complete request body, from the moment the router starts reading it. When exceeded, the request is rejected with `408 Request Timeout` (`PAYLOAD_READ_TIMEOUT`) and the connection is closed.

Both default to `10s`, and `0s` disables them.

```yaml
traffic_shaping:
  router:
    header_read_timeout: 10s
    body_read_timeout: 10s
```

This also fixes how the existing timeouts behaved:

- The header deadline was `request_timeout` plus one second (61s by default), so raising `request_timeout` for slow operations also let clients take that long to send headers. It is now independent, and clients that take longer than `10s` to send headers are disconnected.
- A stalled body used up `request_timeout` and got `504 Gateway Timeout` (`GATEWAY_TIMEOUT`), which blamed the upstream for a slow client. It now gets a `408` once `body_read_timeout` runs out, as long as that is shorter than `request_timeout`.
- The coprocessor `router.request` stage with `include_body` reads the body before `request_timeout` starts, so that read had no deadline at all. `body_read_timeout` now applies to it.

`header_read_timeout` runs before `request_timeout` starts, so the two add up.

`body_read_timeout` runs within `request_timeout`, so it only takes effect when it is shorter, except in the coprocessor `router.request` stage.

If clients upload large bodies over slow connections, consider to raise `body_read_timeout`.

Closes https://github.com/graphql-hive/router/issues/1690

name: hive-router 0.3.4 (2026-10-12)

## Features

### Refresh the remote JWKS when a token's `kid` is unknown

A token signed with a freshly rotated key was rejected until the next `polling_interval` tick. With `refresh_on_unknown_kid` set on a remote JWKS provider, an unknown `kid` re-fetches the JWKS right away. The value is the minimum time between two such re-fetches, so concurrent misses share one fetch and arbitrary `kid`s cannot hammer the endpoint. It must be at least `1s`. Disabled by default.

```yaml
jwt:
  jwks_providers:
    - source: remote
      url: https://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json
      refresh_on_unknown_kid: 30s
```

## Fixes

### Fix `@requires` fields from an entity resolved to `null`

When the subgraph providing a `@requires` field returned `null` for the entity, the router could skip the call that needed that field, and silently drop data.

```graphql
type FavoritesPage @key(fields: "__typename") {
  petCount: Int # from `favorites`
  searchBox: SearchBox! @requires(fields: "petCount") # from `search`
}
```

```graphql
query {
  favoritesPage {
    searchBox {
      placeholder
    }
  }
}
```

Before: `favorites` answered `_entities: [null]`, so the page had no `petCount`. The router left the page out of the call to `search`, `searchBox` was missing, and being non-null, it turned the whole page into `null`, without an error:

```json
{ "data": { "favoritesPage": null } }
```

After: an entity is left out only when none of its keys in that subgraph is complete, as the subgraph can't find it then. A missing `@requires` field is sent as `null`, so `search` gets `{ "__typename": "FavoritesPage", "petCount": null }`:

```json
{ "data": { "favoritesPage": { "searchBox": { "placeholder": "Find a pet" } } } }
```

With a key other than `__typename`, the entity was already sent, without the field. It now has the field, set to `null`.

Closes https://github.com/graphql-hive/router/issues/1669

## Fixes

### Avoid duplicate built-in directive definitions in introspection

Supergraphs that already define a built-in directive, like `@oneOf` (emitted by composition whenever a subgraph uses it), no longer end up with that directive defined twice in the consumer schema.

### Allow `@deprecated` on arguments in introspection results

The router's built-in `@deprecated` definition now includes the `ARGUMENT_DEFINITION` location, as the GraphQL spec requires.

### Fix type conditions on a list of an `@interfaceObject`

Queries with a type condition on a list of an `@interfaceObject`, like `friends { ... on User { name } }`, no longer fail with `No paths found for selection item`.

### Faster Processing of Large Subgraph Responses

The Router no longer sorts the fields of every object in a subgraph response. Objects now keep the order the subgraph sent them in, and the Router finds each field by checking the next one first, since responses follow the order of the query.

This removes a sort per object and a search per field. In our test with a single subgraph returning a 2.8MB response, the time the Router spends on each request dropped by about 10%, and throughput increased by about 5%.

### Validate list literals in more positions

Validation now checks the items of a list literal whose type is a non-null list. For example, `query ($v: [Color]! = [PURPLE])` is rejected when `PURPLE` is not a `Color` value. Before, those items were not checked, so an invalid default was only caught when it was used, or was sent to the subgraph unchecked.

A list literal in a position that doesn't expect a list, like `query ($v: Color = [RED])` or `query ($v: Int = [1])`, is now rejected with a `ValuesOfCorrectType` error. Custom scalars still accept any literal, as described by the GraphQL specification.

### Keep `@provides` fields on the path that provides them

Fields made available by `@provides` could leak to another field returning the same type, like `Store.orders` getting the fields `User.orders` provides. The planner then skipped a fetch it needed. Provided fields now only count on the path of the field that provides them.

### Fix extra fetches for `@requires` after an entity hop

- `@requires` after an entity hop no longer adds an extra fetch to the same subgraph ([#1539](https://github.com/graphql-hive/router/issues/1539)).
- Aliased `@requires` fields with different arguments (like `price(currency: USD)` and `price(currency: EUR)`) now get the right values after an entity hop.

Closes https://github.com/graphql-hive/router/issues/1539

### Use `@provides` fields for `@requires`

When the fields a `@requires` needs are made available by a `@provides` on the way, the field is now fetched together with them, from the same subgraph. Previously the planner ignored the provided fields and made extra `_entities` calls to get them again.

### Fix `@requires` on an object of the same type nested in an entity call

A `@requires` field on an object nested inside an entity of the same type, like `user { other { label } }` where both `user` and `other` are a `User`, no longer fails with `MissingPathInSelection`.

When a field returning a union was progressively overridden (`@override(from: ..., label: ...)`), the overriding subgraph was still used when the label was off. The label is now respected, like it is for other fields.

Errors for invalid variable values now use the graphql-js wording, name the variable, and point to the invalid list item. For example, `$input: [String!]` given `[0, 1]` now returns:


## Breaking Changes

### Validate input object variables

Variable values of input object types are now validated before the operation runs, as the GraphQL spec requires. Before, any value was accepted and forwarded to the subgraphs as-is.

The Router now rejects an input object variable when:

- the value is not an object: `Expected value of type "ReviewInput" to be an object, found: "great".`
- a required field is missing (a non-null field without a default value): `Expected value of type "ReviewInput" to include required field "stars", found: { comment: "great" }.`
- it contains a field the type doesn't define: `Expected value of type "ReviewInput" not to include unknown field "rating", found: { stars: 5, rating: 5 }.`
- a field's value is invalid for its type. The error points to the field, including inside nested objects and lists: `Variable "$review" has invalid value at .tags[1]: String cannot represent a non string value: 1`

Field default values are still applied by the subgraph: the Router forwards the object as sent. The ensures the subgraph has the ability to identify a non-provided variable.

### Validate `@oneOf` input object variables

Variable values of `@oneOf` input object types are now validated before the operation runs. A value must set exactly one field, and that field must not be `null`. Before, any value was accepted and forwarded to the subgraphs.

For example, `{"input": {}}`, `{"input": {"a": "abc", "b": 123}}` and `{"input": {"a": null}}` are now rejected with:

```
Variable "$input" has invalid value: Within OneOf Input Object type "OneOfInput", exactly one field must be specified, and the value for that field must be non-null.
```

This also applies to `@oneOf` objects nested in other input objects or lists, and to variable default values.

Closes https://github.com/graphql-hive/router/issues/1390

## Fixes

### Avoid duplicate built-in directive definitions in introspection

Supergraphs that already define a built-in directive, like `@oneOf` (emitted by composition whenever a subgraph uses it), no longer end up with that directive defined twice in the consumer schema.

### Allow `@deprecated` on arguments in introspection results

The router's built-in `@deprecated` definition now includes the `ARGUMENT_DEFINITION` location, as the GraphQL spec requires.

### Accept `variables=null` in GET requests

A GET request with `variables=null` in the query string no longer fails with `400 Failed to parse GraphQL variables JSON`. Like `"variables": null` in a POST body, it now means the operation has no variables, so their default values apply.

### Validate the range of `Int` literals

`ValuesOfCorrectType` validation rule now rejects `Int` literals outside the 32-bit range, for example `query ($v: Int = 2147483648)`, with `Int cannot represent non 32-bit signed integer value: 2147483648`.

### Fix type conditions on a list of an `@interfaceObject`

Queries with a type condition on a list of an `@interfaceObject`, like `friends { ... on User { name } }`, no longer fail with `No paths found for selection item`.

### Faster Processing of Large Subgraph Responses

The Router no longer sorts the fields of every object in a subgraph response. Objects now keep the order the subgraph sent them in, and the Router finds each field by checking the next one first, since responses follow the order of the query.

This removes a sort per object and a search per field. In our test with a single subgraph returning a 2.8MB response, the time the Router spends on each request dropped by about 10%, and throughput increased by about 5%.

### Validate list literals in more positions

Validation now checks the items of a list literal whose type is a non-null list. For example, `query ($v: [Color]! = [PURPLE])` is rejected when `PURPLE` is not a `Color` value. Before, those items were not checked, so an invalid default was only caught when it was used, or was sent to the subgraph unchecked.

A list literal in a position that doesn't expect a list, like `query ($v: Color = [RED])` or `query ($v: Int = [1])`, is now rejected with a `ValuesOfCorrectType` error. Custom scalars still accept any literal, as described by the GraphQL specification.

Validation now enforces the GraphQL spec's rules for `@oneOf` input objects in operations:

- `ValuesOfCorrectType` rejects a `@oneOf` literal that doesn't set exactly one field (`OneOf Input Object "OneOfInput" must specify exactly one key.`), or sets it to `null` (`Field "OneOfInput.a" must be non-null.`). This covers arguments and variable default values.
- `VariablesInAllowedPosition` rejects a nullable variable used as the field of a `@oneOf` literal, such as `query ($a: String) { field(input: { a: $a }) }`, even when the variable has a default value (`Variable "$a" is of type "String" but must be non-nullable to be used for OneOf Input Object "OneOfInput".`).

### Keep `@provides` fields on the path that provides them

Fields made available by `@provides` could leak to another field returning the same type, like `Store.orders` getting the fields `User.orders` provides. The planner then skipped a fetch it needed. Provided fields now only count on the path of the field that provides them.

### Fix extra fetches for `@requires` after an entity hop

- `@requires` after an entity hop no longer adds an extra fetch to the same subgraph ([#1539](https://github.com/graphql-hive/router/issues/1539)).
- Aliased `@requires` fields with different arguments (like `price(currency: USD)` and `price(currency: EUR)`) now get the right values after an entity hop.

Closes https://github.com/graphql-hive/router/issues/1539

### Use `@provides` fields for `@requires`

When the fields a `@requires` needs are made available by a `@provides` on the way, the field is now fetched together with them, from the same subgraph. Previously the planner ignored the provided fields and made extra `_entities` calls to get them again.

### Fix `@requires` on an object of the same type nested in an entity call

A `@requires` field on an object nested inside an entity of the same type, like `user { other { label } }` where both `user` and `other` are a `User`, no longer fails with `MissingPathInSelection`.

Scalar variable values are now checked and validation using the following rules:

- `Int` accepts only 32-bit integers. A value like `2147483648` is now rejected with `Int cannot represent non 32-bit signed integer value: 2147483648`, instead of being forwarded to the subgraph.
- `ID` now accepts integers as well as strings, as the GraphQL spec requires. This also fixes operations like `query ($id: ID = 1)`, which failed whenever `$id` was omitted.
- `Float` now accepts every JSON number, including integers larger than `9223372036854775807`.
- `Int` and `ID` still reject JSON numbers written as floats, like `1.0` or `1e3`. Error messages now print these values with their `.0` (`Int cannot represent non-integer value: 1.0`).

### Fix progressive `@override` on fields returning a union

When a field returning a union was progressively overridden (`@override(from: ..., label: ...)`), the overriding subgraph was still used when the label was off. The label is now respected, like it is for other fields.

### Variable Coercion Errors Follow the GraphQL Spec

```

```

Values in these messages are printed the way graphql-js prints them (for example `[1]`), not as internal router values. Errors caused by a variable's default value say `has invalid default value`.

As allowed by the September 2025 GraphQL spec (`query ("The user ID" $id: ID!) { ... }`)

name: hive-router 0.2.19 (2026-09-23)
body:
## Features

### Router overhead metrics

Two new histograms report how much of a request's latency is the router's own work versus time spent waiting on external services:

- `hive.router.request.overhead.duration` - the request duration (`http.server.request.duration`) minus the time the request spent waiting on external services. This is the latency the router adds on top of your upstreams: parsing, validation, planning, response merging, plugins.
- `hive.router.request.external_wait.duration` - the time the request spent waiting on at least one external service.

The following are considered "external" and count as waiting:

- Persisted document fetches from the Hive CDN on a cache miss also count as waiting

- Subgraph calls 

- Co-processor calls

They are not recorded for streamed responses (subscriptions, incremental delivery), whose subgraph waits continue after the response headers are sent.

With explicit histogram buckets (the default), `hive.router.request.overhead.duration` uses fine-grained boundaries from 100µs to 1s instead of the shared `seconds` buckets, since router overhead is typically sub-millisecond.

Closes https://github.com/graphql-hive/router/issues/1579

## Fixes

### Export numeric span attributes as integers

Some span attributes were exported as strings, even though the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions define them as integers. Filters that compare numbers, such as tail-sampling policies or TraceQL queries like `span.http.response.status_code >= 500`, did not match these attributes.

The following attributes are now exported as integers:

- `http.response.status_code`
- `http.request.body.size` and `http.response.body.size`
- `server.port`, `client.port` and `network.peer.port`
- `hive.graphql.error.count`
- `cost.estimated` and `cost.actual`

`error.type` on HTTP spans is now always the bare status code as a string, such as `"500"`, as the semantic conventions require. Previously it was sometimes an integer, and 5xx responses recorded the full reason phrase, such as `"500 Internal Server Error"`.

body:
## Features

### Configurable cache TTL and TTI

In-memory caches now support time-based expiry alongside `max_entries`:

```yaml
cache:
  router:
    parsing:
      max_entries: 1000
      time_to_live: 30m
      time_to_idle: 5m
  supergraph:
    validation:
      max_entries: 1000
      time_to_idle: 5m
    normalization:
      max_entries: 1000
      time_to_idle: 5m
    query_plans:
      max_entries: 1000
      time_to_idle: 5m
```

Both `time_to_live` and `time_to_idle` are optional and disabled by default, preserving the existing LRU-only behavior.

- `time_to_live` expires an entry after a fixed duration from its creation or last update, even if it is frequently accessed.
- `time_to_idle` expires an entry after it has not been read or updated for the configured duration.

When both are configured, the entry expires as soon as either condition is met.

Plugins can override each expiry setting independently for every supergraph variant.
Any expiry left unspecified inherits its value from the router configuration.
Overriding one setting does not affect the others.
To explicitly disable an expiry configured at the router level, set that expiry to `None`.

```rust
let mut options = SupergraphOptions::default();
options.cache.query_plans.set_time_to_idle(Some(Duration::from_secs(300)));
options.cache.query_plans.set_time_to_live(None);
```

name: hive-router 0.2.16 (2026-09-17)
body:
## Features

### Configurable cache limits

In-memory cache limits are now configurable:

```yaml
cache:
  router:
    parsing:
      max_entries: 1000
  supergraph:
    validation:
      max_entries: 1000
    normalization:
      max_entries: 1000
    query_plans:
      max_entries: 1000
```

`cache.router` applies once per router process, while `cache.supergraph` applies to each served supergraph variant.

Plugins creating additional supergraph variants can override their cache limits with `SupergraphOptions::cache`:

```rust
let mut options = SupergraphOptions::default();
options.cache.query_plans.set_max_entries(100);
```

Unset values inherit from `cache.supergraph` config or the default values.

### Named supergraphs, surfaced in logs, traces and metrics

Every `Supergraph` now carries a human-readable `name`. The supergraph loaded from the router configuration (`supergraph.source`) is named `default`. Plugins that construct their own supergraphs - for example to serve a different schema variant per tenant or feature flag - give each one a name, and that name is what the router reports when describing which supergraph handled a request.

### Plugin API

`Supergraph::from_sdl` and `Supergraph::from_document` take the name as a new, required first argument:

```rust
// before
let variant = Supergraph::from_document(document, options)?;

// after
let variant = Supergraph::from_document("my-supergraph", document, options)?;
```

#### Logging

The request summary line (`router::request` target) reports the name of the supergraph that processed the request:

- **Added** `supergraph_name` - the selected supergraph's name, e.g. `"default"` or the name a plugin chose. It is absent when the request was rejected before a supergraph was selected.
- **Removed** `supergraph_identifier` - the internal numeric id previously printed in its place. It was not stable across restarts or reloads and was never meaningful to operators.

Example (JSON format):

```json
{"level":"INFO","target":"router::request","operation_type":"query","status_code":200,"supergraph_name":"default","duration_ms":12,...}
```

#### Traces

The `graphql.operation` span gains the attribute:

- `hive.supergraph.name` - the selected supergraph's name.

It is recorded as soon as the supergraph is selected, for both HTTP and WebSocket (`graphql-ws`) operations.

Only the operation span carries it; child spans (parse, validate, plan, subgraph calls) are unchanged and can be attributed to a supergraph through their parent.

#### Metrics

A `supergraph.name` label is added to:

- `http.server.request.duration`
- `hive.router.graphql.errors_total`

Both now break down by supergraph, so a deployment serving several schema variants from one router can chart latency and error rates per variant.

For `http.server.request.duration` the label is omitted on requests that failed before a supergraph was selected (e.g. malformed HTTP requests).

For `hive.router.graphql.errors_total` it is omitted for errors raised before selection.

Closes https://github.com/graphql-hive/router/issues/1565

body:
## Features

### Add `process_variables` to Hive Console usage reporting

By default, usage reports mark every field of an input-object variable's declared type as used, because the SDK cannot know which fields a client actually sends.

With `telemetry.hive.usage_reporting.process_variables: true`, the router reads request's raw variables (taken before coercion) with its usage report, and the usage report lists only the input fields present in the payload.

In either mode, the variable values are never sent to Hive Console, only schema coordinates.

Defaults to `false`;

Closes https://github.com/graphql-hive/router/issues/1488

## Fixes

### Mark HTTP 200 GraphQL errors as failed telemetry spans

GraphQL responses can contain errors while still returning an HTTP 200 status. These responses previously left `graphql.operation` spans without an error status and marked the root `http.server` span as successful. Observability platforms could therefore report a 0% service error rate even while the router was returning GraphQL errors.

The router now sets the OpenTelemetry status to `Error` on both the `graphql.operation` span and the root `http.server` span when the GraphQL response contains errors. This allows tracing backends such as Datadog to include these requests in operation-level and service-level error rates without requiring a custom plugin.

Successful 1xx, 2xx, and 3xx root HTTP spans now leave their OpenTelemetry status unset instead of explicitly setting it to `Ok`. This follows the [OpenTelemetry HTTP semantic conventions](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/http/http-spans/#status) and prevents a successful HTTP status from overwriting an error detected while processing the GraphQL response. HTTP 5xx responses continue to set the span status to `Error` and record the status code as `error.type`.

A GraphQL response can contain multiple errors with different codes and types, so the router does not assign a single aggregate `error.type` to the root or operation span. Individual error details continue to be recorded as span events.

This change does not alter the handling of manually supplied `datadog.error` attributes. The Datadog exporter receives the standard OpenTelemetry error status and maps it to Datadog's native span error flag.
